paragraphs: SECTION 5.3.

Dr. Gregory’s Legacy to his daughters is so full of fatherly concern that I approach the task of criticizing it with affectionate respect. Yet this little volume has many attractions to recommend it to the most respectable part of my sex, and so I cannot keep silent about arguments that lend such plausible support to opinions which, in my view, have done the greatest harm to the morals and conduct of the female world.

His easy, familiar style particularly suits the tenor of his advice, and the melancholy tenderness that his respect for the memory of a beloved wife spreads through the whole work makes it very affecting. Yet in many passages there is a noticeable degree of concise elegance that disturbs this sympathy; we stumble upon the author when we expected to meet only the — father.

Besides, since he had two aims, he rarely held steadily to either. He wished to make his daughters amiable, yet he feared that the only result of instilling sentiments which might lead them off the beaten track of ordinary life, without equipping them to act with a matching independence and dignity, would be unhappiness; so he checks the natural flow of his thoughts, and his advice goes neither one way nor the other.
In the preface he tells them a sad truth, “that they will hear, at least once in their lives, the genuine sentiments of a man, who has no interest in deceiving them.”

Unhappy woman! What can be expected of you, when the beings on whom you are said by nature to depend for reason and support all have an interest in deceiving you! This is the root of the evil that has spread a corroding mildew over all your virtues and, blighting your opening faculties in the bud, has made you the weak thing you are! It is this separate interest — this insidious state of warfare — that undermines morality and divides mankind!

If love has made some women wretched — how many more has the cold, meaningless traffic of gallantry made vain and useless! Yet this heartless attention to the sex is thought so manly, so polite, that until society is organized very differently, I fear, this relic of gothic manners will not give way to a more reasonable and affectionate mode of conduct. Moreover, to strip it of its imaginary dignity, I must point out that in the most civilized states of Europe this lip-service is extremely widespread, and goes together with an extreme looseness of morals. In Portugal, the country I particularly have in mind, it takes precedence over the most serious moral obligations; for a man is seldom assassinated while he is in the company of a woman. The savage hand of violence is unnerved by this chivalrous spirit; and if the stroke of vengeance cannot be held back — the lady is begged to pardon the rudeness and to go in peace, though she may be spattered with her husband’s or her brother’s blood.
I shall not discuss his strictures on religion here, since I plan to treat that subject in a chapter of its own.

Many of his remarks on behaviour are very sensible, yet I disapprove of them entirely, because he seems to me to start, so to speak, at the wrong end. A cultivated understanding and an affectionate heart will never need starched rules of decorum; they will produce something more substantial than mere seemliness; while without understanding, the behaviour he recommends would be sheer affectation. Decorum, indeed, is the one thing needful! Nature is to be supplanted by decorum, and all simplicity and variety of character banished from the female world. Yet what good purpose can such superficial counsel serve? Admittedly, it is far easier to prescribe one way of behaving or another than to set the reason to work; but once the mind has been stocked with useful knowledge and strengthened by exercise, its guidance can safely be trusted to regulate behaviour.

Why, for example, give the following warning, when artifice of any kind must contaminate the mind? And why tangle the great motives of action, which reason and religion alike urge, with pitiful worldly dodges and sleight-of-hand tricks meant to earn the applause of gaping, tasteless fools? “Be even cautious in displaying your good sense.* It will be thought you assume a superiority over the rest of the company — But if you happen to have any learning keep it a profound secret, especially from the men, who generally look with a jealous and malignant eye on a woman of great parts, and a cultivated understanding.” If, as he later observes, men of real merit are above such baseness, why must the conduct of the entire sex be tuned to please fools — or men who, having little claim to respect as individuals, choose to close ranks in their phalanx? Men, indeed, whose only superiority is that of sex are certainly very excusable for insisting on the superiority they all share.
(*Footnote. Let women once acquire good sense — and if it deserves the name, it will teach them how to use it; otherwise, what use will it be?)
If it were right always to adopt the tone of the company, rules of behaviour would be endless; for with the key changing constantly, a FLAT would often pass for a NATURAL note.

Surely the wiser advice would have been for women to improve themselves until they rose above the fumes of vanity, and then to leave public opinion to come round — for where are rules of accommodation to end? The narrow path of truth and virtue swerves neither right nor left; it runs straight ahead, and those who follow it in earnest may leap over many decorous prejudices without leaving modesty behind them. Purify the heart and give the head work to do, and I venture to predict that nothing in the behaviour will give offence.

Whenever I see the fashionable air that so many young people are eager to acquire, it reminds me of the studied poses in certain modern prints, copied with tasteless servility from antique statues: the soul has been left out, and nothing that could properly be called character binds the parts together. This varnish of fashion, which rarely clings very closely to good sense, may dazzle the weak; but if nature is left to itself, it will seldom disgust the wise. Besides, if a woman has sense enough not to pretend to anything she does not in some measure understand, she has no need to resolve to hide her talents under a bushel. Let things take their natural course, and all will be well.

It is this system of dissimulation, running through the whole volume, that I despise. Women are always to SEEM to be this and that — yet virtue might address them in the words of Hamlet: “Seems! I know not seems! — Have that within that passeth show!”

The same tone recurs, for in another place, after recommending delicacy (without drawing sufficient distinctions), he adds, “The men will complain of your reserve. They will assure you that a franker behaviour would make you more amiable. But, trust me, they are not sincere when they tell you so. I acknowledge that on some occasions it might render you more agreeable as companions, but it would make you less amiable as women: an important distinction, which many of your sex are not aware of.”

This desire to be women at every moment is the very self-consciousness that degrades the sex. I must repeat, with emphasis, something I said before: except with a lover, it would be well if they were simply agreeable or rational companions. But on this point his advice even contradicts a passage which I intend to quote with the most marked approval.

“The sentiment, that a woman may allow all innocent freedoms, provided her virtue is secure, is both grossly indelicate and dangerous, and has proved fatal to many of your sex.” I agree with this opinion completely. Any man or woman of feeling must always want to assure the one they love that the caresses received and returned with pleasure are those of the individual, not of the sex, and that what is moved is the heart rather than the senses. Without this natural delicacy, love turns into a selfish personal gratification that soon degrades the character.

I carry this sentiment further still. Affection, when love is out of the question, justifies many personal endearments which, flowing naturally from an innocent heart, give life to behaviour; but physical familiarity prompted by appetite, gallantry or vanity is despicable. When a man squeezes the hand of a pretty woman he has never seen before as he hands her into a carriage, she will regard such an impertinent liberty as an insult, if she has any true delicacy, instead of being flattered by this meaningless homage to beauty. These are the privileges of friendship, or of the momentary homage the heart pays to virtue when it suddenly flashes into view — mere high spirits have no claim to the kindnesses of affection.

Since I wish the affections to be nourished by what now nourishes vanity, I would gladly persuade my sex to act on simpler principles. If they deserve love they will win it, even if no one ever tells them that “The power of a fine woman over the hearts of men, of men of the finest parts, is even beyond what she conceives.”

I have already remarked on his narrow cautions about duplicity, female softness and delicacy of constitution; he rings the changes on these without ceasing — more decorously than Rousseau, it is true, yet it all comes back to the same point, and whoever takes the trouble to analyze these sentiments will find that the first principles are not quite so delicate as the superstructure built on them.
The subject of amusements is treated too briefly, but in the same spirit.

When I come to treat friendship, love and marriage, it will be seen that we differ materially in opinion. I shall not, then, anticipate what I have to say on these important subjects, but will confine my remarks to their general tenor: to that cautious family prudence, to those narrow views of partial, unenlightened affection, which shut out pleasure and improvement by vainly trying to ward off sorrow and error — and which, by guarding the heart and mind in this way, destroy all their energy as well. It is far better to be often deceived than never to trust; to be disappointed in love than never to love; to lose a husband’s fondness than to forfeit his esteem.

How happy it would be for the world — and so, of course, for individuals — if all this fruitless anxiety to secure worldly happiness on a narrow plan were turned into an eager wish to improve the understanding. “Wisdom is the principal thing: THEREFORE get wisdom; and with all thy gettings get understanding.” “How long ye simple ones, will ye love simplicity, and hate knowledge?” So Wisdom says to the daughters of men!
